newsitem.title: kenya: Foreign aid workers quit east Zaire camp, town.
newsitem.headline: Foreign aid workers quit east Zaire camp, town.

text.p: The last foreign aid workers pulled out by air on Friday from the biggest refugee camp in eastern Zaire and a nearby town because of concerns about their security.
Aid officials told Reuters about 20 United Nations and non-U.N. aid agency staff from the town of Lubutu and Tingi Tingi refugee camp were flown to the town of Kisangani on three flights.
"There are no international aid workers now left in Tingi Tingi or Lubutu," said an aid official, speaking by telephone from Kisangani. "But national (Zairean) staff remain to keep things going."
"The international staff were pulled out to reassess the situation but they are still planning to go back," he added.

Zairean troops are battling Tutsi rebels in the country's east, part of which is now under rebel control. On Thursday, aid workers said refugees fled Amisi camp because there was fighting near there. Amisi is 80 km (50 miles) from Lubutu towards the rebel-held east.
The foreign aid workers decided to quit Lubutu after apparently panicky Zairean government soldiers fired in the air for five hours on Friday and demanded money and vehicles from aid agencies.

Troops surrounded a U.N. compound and refused to let six Zairean World Food Programme (WFP) staff leave and beat up the radio operator. The problem was defused when the soldiers realised the aid workers had no money and left, officials said.
The WFP radio operator was later flown to Kisangani.
A WFP official who flew to Lubutu and visited Tingi Tingi on Friday said all the estimated 120,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees were still there and had not prepared to leave, contrary to earlier reports.
"There is no sense of movement from Tingi Tingi, no one seemed to be packing up. The nutritional centres are still operating and everything appeared pretty normal," he said.
He said he was told by refugees that tens of thousands of other refugees who fled from Amisi were camped five km (three miles) to the southwest of the camp, seven km (four miles) southeast of Lubutu.
Three Zairean WFP staff who travelled with the refugees from Amisi, which had a population of some 40,000, estimated that large numbers of them were camped just outside Tingi Tingi.
Tingi Tingi is the site of the largest concentration of refugees in eastern Zaire and is 200 km (125 miles) southeast of Kisangani.
Other aid sources said 170 wounded Zairean soldiers were evacuated from Amisi to Lubutu on Thursday and U.N. staff in Kisangani were told to stay in their homes or offices on Friday.
They said large numbers of residents had gone to the governor's office in Kisangani, demanding better security.

Zairean defence officials on Thursday hotly denied rebel claims that advancing rebels were near Lubutu town on the road to Kisangani, headquarters for an army counter-offensive launched on January 20, and Isiro town to the northeast.
Zairean officials said the refugees had been panicked by rumours. "They are fleeing because of rumours," one said.

Relief officials have expressed increasing concern at the plight of hundreds of thousands of Hutus trapped by the fighting after fleeing westwards in December with Rwandan Hutu hardliners, blamed for the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda.

The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, arrived in Kinshasa on Friday. She had hoped to visit Tingi Tingi to meet some of the thousands of refugees near the war zone. It was not clear whether the visit would go ahead.
